Grid page: a number, some text and a formula each sit in a cell of the same grid.

Excel for Absolute Beginners · No. 01
Basics

What Excel Is For

Rows and columns of boxes that add up your numbers.

Let's say you've typed a month of expenses into a column and need the total. Excel is made of rows and columns of boxes called cells. Each cell can hold a number, some text or a formula.

Once your data is in rows and columns, Excel can add it up, sort and filter it, put it in tables, and build charts. It's good for simple sums and for tracking almost any kind of information.

A total you type in yourself stays put when the numbers under it change.

Put the numbers in cells and let Excel do the adding.

DO THIS NOW

Type 25 in cell A1 and press Enter. Then type Milk in cell B1 and press Enter.

Excel for Absolute Beginners · No. 02
Files

Workbooks, Sheets and Cells

The file, its pages, and the name of every box on them.

Let's say someone asks you for the sales file. That file is a workbook, the Excel file you save. A workbook holds sheets, and you can add as many sheets as you want to one workbook.

Each cell has an address made from its column letter and row number, such as B2. Without addresses, you'd have to describe every box as "the box in the third column of the second row" each time you wanted to point at one.

The workbook is the file, the sheet is a page inside it, and B2 names one box.

Excel for Absolute Beginners · No. 03
The screen

A Tour of the Excel Window

The parts of the screen to learn first.

Let's say you've opened Excel for the first time and the screen looks crowded. Three parts do most of the early work.

The ribbon has tabs, such as Home and Insert. Each tab groups related options together, so the buttons you need sit in one place. The formula bar shows the formula in the selected cell, and the Name box sits to its left. Type a cell address in the Name box and press Enter to jump straight to that cell.

The ribbon holds the buttons, and the formula bar shows the formula behind the answer.

Moving

Moving Around the Sheet

Get from the top of a list to the bottom without the mouse.

Let's say you need the last row of a long list. You scroll with the mouse, overshoot, scroll back and lose your place. There's a quicker way.

The arrow keys move one cell at a time. Ctrl with an arrow key jumps to the edge of your data, so Ctrl+Down arrow takes you to the bottom of a list in one press. Ctrl+Home goes back to the start of the sheet, and Ctrl+End goes to the last cell in use.

Ctrl and an arrow key get you to the edge of your data in one press.

Give each part of your work its own page, with a name you'll recognise.

Click the New Sheet plus icon at the bottom of the workbook to add one. Double-click a sheet's tab to rename it, so the name tells you what's inside. Ctrl+Page down moves you to the next sheet.

Give each part of your work its own sheet and its own name.

A number that looks right but won't add up.

Let's say a column of prices looks right, but the total is too small. Some of the numbers are stored as text. Excel usually shows an alert next to the cell, a green triangle warning. SUM ignores text values, so those numbers never reach the total, and nothing looks wrong until you add them up.

Convert them once, and the total is right.

How Excel reads a date you type, and why the same date can look different.

How to tell Excel which cells the next command should use.

A calculation you type into a cell, starting with an equals sign.

Let's say you've worked out a sum on a calculator and typed the answer into a cell. The answer is still sitting there when the numbers change, and nobody notices it's wrong.

A formula does the working for you. Every formula in Excel begins with an equals sign, which tells Excel to work it out rather than store the text.

A formula is a question the cell asks again every time its numbers change.

The typical number in a group, not the total.

The lowest and the highest number in a group.

References

Copying Formulas: Relative References

A copied formula moves its cell addresses with it.

Let's say D1 multiplies a quantity by a price, and the next two rows need the same sum. Typing each formula by hand is slow.

Copy the formula instead. By default, a cell address in a formula is relative, which means Excel measures it from the cell that holds the formula. Copy the formula to another cell and the address moves with it. Copy =B4*C4 from D4 to D5, and D5 reads =B5*C5. The row number moves down with the formula.

Copy it once, and every row gets its own.

Formulas

Locking a Cell With the Dollar Sign

A dollar sign keeps a cell address fixed when you copy.

Let's say a tax rate sits in cell F1, and every row in column B needs to be multiplied by it. Copy the formula down, and the reference to the rate moves with it. The next row points at an empty cell.

Excel formulas can use relative or absolute cell addresses, and Excel can switch a formula between them. Put a dollar sign in front of the column and the row, as in $F$1, and that address stays fixed when you copy.

A dollar sign tells Excel: this one stays put.

DO THIS NOW

In C1, type =B1*$F$1. Copy it down the column, and check that every row still uses F1.

Mixed page: a dollar sign before only the column or only the row fixes that part, and the other part moves when you copy.

References

Mixed References: Lock Only the Column or the Row

Fix the column or the row, and let the other one move.

Let's say one formula has to be copied across and down. Fix the whole address and nothing moves. Leave it open and everything moves.

Put a dollar sign in front of just the column or just the row. $B4 fixes the column, and C$4 fixes the row. Excel calls these mixed references. Copy two cells down and two to the right, and $A1 becomes $A3, while A$1 becomes C$1. The part with the dollar sign stays put, and the other part moves.

The dollar sign marks what stays. The rest moves.

Decisions

Comparing Two Values

A comparison answers TRUE or FALSE.

Let's say you want to know whether one number is bigger than another, and you're checking by eye.

Comparing two values with a comparison symbol gives the answer TRUE or FALSE. The = sign means equal to, > means greater than, and < means less than. Add an = after > or < for greater than or equal to (>=) and less than or equal to (<=). <> means not equal to.

A comparison always gives TRUE or FALSE.

IF page: IF tests a condition and shows one answer if it is true and another if it is false.

Excel for Absolute Beginners · No. 41
Decisions

IF: Making a Decision in a Cell

One formula, two possible answers.

Let's say you're checking costs against a budget, and you want the sheet to say "Over Budget" instead of making you work it out.

IF returns one value if a condition is true and another value if it's false. It takes three parts: the test, what to show if the test is true, and what to show if it's false. =IF(C2>B2,"Over Budget","Within Budget") checks whether C2 is greater than B2, and shows Over Budget if it is. Text in a formula goes in quotation marks.

A # message points at what went wrong.

Let's say a cell shows #DIV/0! and you have no idea what you did wrong.

A small triangle in a cell's top-left corner marks an error.

#DIV/0! means a number is divided by zero, or by a blank cell. #NAME? usually means a typo in the formula name. #REF! means a cell the formula uses isn't valid, often after cells were deleted or pasted over. #VALUE! means something's wrong with how the formula is typed, or with the cells it uses.

Read the message, then look for its cause.

DO THIS NOW

Type 55 in A3 and leave B3 empty. In C3 type =A3/B3 and press Enter. Read the message.

PivotTables

Why PivotTables Exist

A PivotTable answers many questions about one list.

Let's say your sales list is finished. Someone asks for the total by region, so you write a SUMIF. Then they want it by salesperson, then by product. Every new question is another formula to write, check and keep right.

A PivotTable is an Excel tool that calculates, summarises and analyses a list, so you can see comparisons, patterns and trends. The first book called it a summary table. It's the same thing, and from here on this book uses its proper name.

One list can answer many questions.

A PivotTable needs a tidy list with no gaps.

Let's say you're about to build your first PivotTable. Blank rows are exactly what Microsoft says to avoid.

The shape to aim for is a tidy list, like the Sales sheet: one row per sale, one row of headings across the top, and no blank rows or columns inside it. That's a list a PivotTable can read.

Tidy list in, answers out.

Run a short checklist before you build.

Let's say a colleague sends you their sales list and you want to pivot it. You can't tell by looking whether it's in good shape.

Microsoft's advice comes down to a short checklist. Every column has a heading, and no two headings are the same. There's one row of headings, not two. No cells are merged. And no column mixes dates and text.

Tidy the list first, then build.

Know what each part of a finished PivotTable is.

Let's say your PivotTable shows a block of numbers. A number you can't place is a number you can't trust.

Row labels run down the left, column labels run across the top, and the numbers in the middle are your values.

Tidy once, then refresh.

Cleaning the Same Data Every Week

Fix it by hand, and next week you fix it again.

Excel Power Query for Absolute Beginners · No. 02
Power Query

What Power Query Does in Excel

Excel's tool for bringing data in and tidying it.

Let's say you've heard the name and assumed it was for someone else. Power Query is built into Excel, which also calls it Get & Transform. It brings data in and shapes it, say by removing a column.

Microsoft splits the work into four jobs. Connect to the data. Transform it, while the original stays as it was. Combine data from more than one place. Load the result onto a sheet. It's in Excel for Windows, for Mac and for the web.

Connect, transform, combine, load. That's the whole tool.

Every change becomes a named step, run in order.

The Join Kinds in Plain Words

The join kind decides which rows survive.

The Merge box starts on Left outer: every row of the first table stays, and a row with no match gets null. Inner keeps only rows that match in both. Full outer keeps every row of both.

Left anti keeps only first-table rows with no match, to find what's missing. Merging the January and February sales with Products, left outer keeps 31 rows, inner 25 and left anti 6. Inner drops sales without a word.

Left outer keeps everything. Inner keeps only matches.
